job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed only the text you pasted, so I can't tell what the manager's amendment changed. I also haven't checked the cross-references to existing law. Some items below may be deliberate policy choices (the grandfathering, the thresholds, the sunset), so they are worth putting to committee staff as questions rather than errors.

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold:** The 10,000-ton cap applies to "a single vessel," with no aggregation across vessels, affiliates, or a common project. An operator can split recovery among several vessels, each under the cap, and none of them engages in "commercial deep seabed mining."

2. **§2(1)(A), measurement:** The text doesn't say whether "per year" means a calendar year, a rolling 12 months, or a prorated period. It doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry, or whether it is measured at the seabed or at the surface. "Recovery," "polymetallic nodules," and "other mineral resources" are undefined, so it's unclear whether crusts, sulfides, or sediment count. This makes the threshold hard to prove and easy to contest.

3. **§2(1)(A), no "commercial" element:** The definition is purely a tonnage test, so sub-threshold extraction is lawful even if the material is sold. Pilot or test mining just under the cap is allowed, while a large non-commercial research recovery is technically covered.

4. **§2(1)(A), 200-meter depth:** 200 meters is roughly the continental-shelf edge, not "deep" seabed in the usual sense. The test could sweep in shelf and EEZ activity such as sand, gravel, and phosphate extraction, inviting overbreadth and conflict arguments. It also doesn't say where depth is measured (the vessel's position, the site's mean depth, or the shallowest point).

5. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's determination:** "The Secretary" is undefined (Commerce? Interior? NOAA's parent department?). There is no standard beyond "comparable" risk, no notice, rulemaking, or publication requirement, and no statement of whether the determination must precede the conduct. Because §5(b) attaches criminal liability to §3, this invites vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges.

6. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It omits LLCs and partnerships (unless "corporation" is read broadly), trusts, associations, permanent residents, and possibly DC and territorial entities. There is no ownership or control test, so a foreign subsidiary or a reincorporated entity falls outside it.

7. **§3(a), jurisdictional reach:** "Person" and "United States" are undefined, including whether the EEZ, territorial sea, and territories are covered. A non-U.S. entity operating a foreign-flag vessel beyond U.S. waters isn't "in the United States," and there is no flag-vessel hook.

8. **§3(a), no downstream controls:** The bill doesn't reach financing, services, processing, import, landing, or sale of seabed minerals. Extraction can move to a foreign affiliate while the material still enters the U.S. market.

9. **§3(b), "exploration license" undefined:** The text doesn't say who issued the license (NOAA, a foreign government, or the International Seabed Authority). It exempts "mining" under an exploration license, yet exploration licenses typically don't authorize commercial recovery. It is also silent on commercial recovery permits issued before enactment.

10. **§3(b), no limits on the grandfather clause:** There is no volume cap, no duration, and no requirement to stay within the license's terms or area. Renewals, amendments, and transfers aren't addressed, and the clause rewards a rush to obtain licenses before enactment.

11. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** The exemption turns on the "purpose" of an activity, with no definition, scale or volume limit, government approval, or public reporting. It is effectively self-certified and depends on subjective intent, which makes it a possible cover for test mining.

12. **§4(a), "covered vessel" and "operator":** The 5,000-gross-ton floor and the word "equipped" don't track the §3 recovery test. Smaller vessels, chartered vessels, and temporary or modular equipment can avoid registration. "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, or contractor), and foreign-flag vessels aren't addressed.

13. **§4, no penalty for registry violations:** §5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failure to register or file a report has no stated civil or criminal consequence, and the only remedy may be a general false-statement statute. There is also no registration deadline.

14. **§4(b), reports:** The bill doesn't specify required content (tonnage, location, depth, dates), the form of "certified," or any audit, inspection, or recordkeeping authority. It gives NOAA no explicit rulemaking authority or funding and says nothing about public disclosure or confidentiality, so NOAA would struggle to verify the threshold.

15. **§5(a), civil enforcement mechanics:** The bill doesn't say which agency assesses penalties, whether through an administrative process or a civil action by the Attorney General. It lacks penalty factors, inflation adjustment, injunctive relief, and vessel or proceeds forfeiture. "Any person" is undefined, so parent-company and officer liability is unclear.

16. **§5(a) vs. §8, date conflict:** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later, and §3 can't be violated before then. This is either surplusage or an invitation to litigate retroactivity and notice. It is likely a drafting error.

17. **§5(b), "willfully":** The bill doesn't say whether willfulness means knowing the conduct is unlawful or just knowing the facts. Combined with the open-ended §2(1)(B) determination and the threshold ambiguities, this makes prosecution difficult and invites vagueness defenses. There is no organizational-liability or forfeiture provision.

18. **§6, negotiation mandate:** It's unclear whether "not later than 18 months" governs starting negotiations, concluding them, or reaching an agreement. There is no reporting requirement, consequence, or definition of "equivalent." The clock runs from enactment, not the effective date, and the bill has no leverage against non-participating states.

19. **§7(a), termination mechanism:** "Serious harm" is undefined. The bill doesn't require the National Academies to produce a report or set a timeline or funding for one, and "acting on a report" doesn't require a favorable one. A joint resolution is subject to presidential signature or veto override, and there are no expedited procedures. The legal effect of a "finding" versus a repeal is unclear.

20. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal conflict:** The sunset ends the Act after 10 years whatever the science shows, which makes the "until Congress finds" condition largely meaningless. Because of the 180-day delay, the effective prohibition lasts about 9.5 years. Industry can plan around the expiration date.

21. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The Act has no provision preserving enforcement for violations committed before expiration. Pending or future cases could face abatement arguments, since the general saving statute is clearer for repeals than for sunsets.

22. **§8, 180-day delay and no wind-down:** Nothing prohibits ramping up operations before the effective date. The bill doesn't address operations ongoing on that date without a license, stockpiled material, or equipment already deployed.

23. **Whole bill, relationship to existing law:** The Act neither amends nor expressly overrides the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. ch. 26) or the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The 200-meter test overlaps the latter. Parties holding permits or leases under those statutes could argue conflict or implied authorization. Counsel should check this.

24. **Whole bill, missing standard provisions:** There is no severability clause, which matters given the exposure of §2(1)(B). There is also no judicial review or citizen-suit provision, no authorization of appropriations, and no general rulemaking authority. "Secretary," "person," "United States," "operator," "recovery," and "serious harm" are all undefined.

**Highest impact for the markup:** items 1 (vessel splitting), 6–8 (foreign-entity and downstream gaps), 9–10 (open-ended grandfathering), 13 (unenforceable registry), 16 (date conflict), and 19–20 (the ban's end conditions).

If it would help, I can turn these into a one-page markup-preview table or a list of likely amendments by section.
